title: Food safety and preserving
summary: Temperature limits, how long food keeps when the power fails, safe cooking temperatures, and which foods need a pressure canner because of botulism. Also drying, salting and smoking basics, shelf lives of stored staples, signs of an unsafe can, and storing drinking water.

steps.text: Power out, or food left on the counter? Check the temperature rules and the outage table, then throw out anything doubtful.
steps.warn: When in doubt, throw it out. Spoiled food can look and smell normal.

steps.text: Canning vegetables, meat, fish or soup? Use a pressure canner and a tested recipe, and take altitude adjustments from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning.
steps.warn: Never use a boiling-water canner for low-acid food. Botulism toxin gives no warning by smell, taste or colour.

steps.text: Look over any can or jar against the unsafe list before opening it. Do not taste-test.
Plan water and staples from the amounts and shelf-life table. Date everything and use the oldest first.

notes:
## Temperature rules
| What | Metric | Imperial |
|---|---|---|
| Danger zone, where bacteria multiply fast | 4 to 60 °C | 40 to 140 °F |
| Fridge at or below | 4 °C | 40 °F |
| Freezer at or below | -18 °C | 0 °F |

- Keep food in the danger zone no more than 2 hours, or 1 hour on a hot day (Health Canada).
- Spoiled food can look and smell fine. When in doubt, throw it out (Health Canada).

## Fridge and freezer in a power outage
| Door kept shut | Food stays safe about |
|---|---|
| Fridge | 4 hours (Health Canada, Ready.gov) |
| Full freezer | 48 hours (Health Canada, Ready.gov) |
| Half-full freezer | 24 hours (Health Canada) |

- Keep a thermometer in each. Fridge food at 4 °C (40 °F) or warmer for 2 hours or more goes in the trash (Ready.gov).
- Frozen food with ice crystals, or still fridge-cold, can be refrozen. Cook it to a safe temperature (Health Canada).
- Discard anything with an odd colour or smell, or that sat at room temperature 2 hours or more (Health Canada).

## Safe internal cooking temperatures (Health Canada)
| Food | °C | °F |
|---|---|---|
| Ground beef, veal, lamb, pork; pork cuts | 71 | 160 |
| Beef, veal, lamb pieces, medium-rare | 63 | 145 |
| Poultry pieces, ground poultry, stuffing, egg dishes, leftovers, most game | 74 | 165 |
| Whole poultry | 82 | 180 |
| Fish | 70 | 158 |
| Shellfish | 74 | 165 |

US guidance gives 63 °C (145 °F) plus a 3-minute rest for roasts, steaks and chops, pork included, and 74 °C (165 °F) for whole poultry (NDSU). When unsure, use the higher figure. Probe the thickest part, away from bone (Health Canada).

## Canning: pressure or water bath?
| Food | Method |
|---|---|
| High-acid, pH 4.6 or lower: fruit, jam, pickles, sauerkraut, tomatoes with added lemon juice or vinegar | Boiling-water canner, 100 °C at sea level (Health Canada) |
| Low-acid, pH above 4.6: most vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, soup, milk, sauces with meat | Pressure canner only, at the pressure for your gauge and altitude (table below), 116 to 121 °C (240 to 250 °F) (NCHFP) |

**Why:** botulism spores survive boiling. In a sealed jar of moist, low-acid food with under 2% oxygen, at 4 to 49 °C (40 to 120 °F), they make a deadly toxin within 3 to 4 days (NCHFP). Botulism does not change colour, smell or taste. Symptoms start 12 to 36 hours after eating: double vision, dry throat, vomiting, fatigue, then paralysis. Get emergency help (Health Canada).

- Use current tested recipes. Never change times, pressures, jar sizes or ingredients. Use new lids (Health Canada).
- Vent a pressure canner 10 minutes before pressurizing. If pressure drops, restart the full time (NCHFP).
- Check dial gauges yearly. Replace one that is off by more than 2 lb (NCHFP).

**Altitude:** water boils at lower temperatures as you climb (NCHFP).

| Height | Water boils at |
|---|---|
| Sea level | 100 °C (212 °F) |
| 610 m (2,000 ft) | 98 °C (208 °F) |
| 1,830 m (6,000 ft) | 94 °C (201 °F) |
| 3,050 m (10,000 ft) | 90 °C (194 °F) |

From about 300 m (1,000 ft) up, lengthen boiling-water times and raise canner pressure. Never can low-acid food below the pressure for your altitude: under-processing risks botulism.

| Altitude | Weighted gauge | Dial gauge |
|---|---|---|
| Up to 305 m (1,000 ft) | 10 psi | 11 psi |
| 305 to 610 m (1,000 to 2,000 ft) | 15 psi | 11 psi |
| 610 to 1,220 m (2,000 to 4,000 ft) | 15 psi | 12 psi |
| 1,220 to 1,830 m (4,000 to 6,000 ft) | 15 psi | 13 psi |
| 1,830 to 2,440 m (6,000 to 8,000 ft) | 15 psi | 14 psi |

These are the usual USDA pressures for most low-acid foods (NCHFP, UC ANR); the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning gives the exact time and pressure for each food. Have a dial gauge tested yearly.

## Drying, salting, smoking
- **Vegetables:** oven at 60 to 63 °C (140 to 145 °F), door ajar 5 to 15 cm (2 to 6 in), fan nearby. Dry until brittle (NDSU). Most need blanching first (Clemson).
- **Fruit:** dry to about 20% moisture, then jar loosely for 7 to 10 days, shaking daily. Condensation means dry more (NCHFP).
- **Keeping dried food:** cool, dark, dry, airtight. Fruit lasts about 1 year at 16 °C (60 °F), vegetables about half that. Discard mould (NCHFP).
- **Jerky:** heat meat to 71 °C (160 °F) and poultry to 74 °C (165 °F) first, then dry at 54 to 60 °C (130 to 140 °F). Keeps 1 to 2 months at room temperature (USDA FSIS, UW-Extension).
- **Salting:** salt draws out water, so most spoilage bacteria cannot grow, but not all (NCHFP, K-State). Cure meat at 0 to 4 °C (32 to 40 °F), about 7 days per inch of thickness. Nitrite is toxic in excess: weigh it, never guess (Mississippi State).
- **Smoking:** hot smoking runs near 104 °C (220 °F) and cooks meat. Cold smoking stays under 38 °C (100 °F), does not cook it, and needs a cure and cold storage (Minnesota Agriculture, Mississippi State). Smoke is only a bonus preservative (NCHFP). Follow a tested extension recipe for any cure.

## Shelf life of staples (quality, not safety)
| Food | Typical pantry life (NDSU) |
|---|---|
| Rice, white | 1 to 2 years |
| Dried beans | 12 months |
| White flour | 6 to 12 months unopened; frozen, indefinite |
| Whole-wheat flour | 3 to 6 months unopened |
| Vegetable oil | 6 months unopened, 3 to 5 opened |
| Store-bought cans | 12 to 18 months for most; canned meat up to 5 years |

- Sealed, oxygen-free white rice at 4 °C (40 °F) or colder can last 25 to 30 years (USU).
- Store-bought cans stay safe while the seal holds; quality lasts to the date code, often 2 to 5 years (USU).
- Home-canned food: best within 1 year (Health Canada), use within 2 (USU).
- Keep food at a steady 4 to 21 °C (40 to 70 °F), dark, dry, off the floor. Never let cans freeze (USU).

## Is this can or jar unsafe?
Throw it out, untasted, if it bulges, leaks, is badly dented or rusty, has a loose or broken seal, spurts when opened, or smells or looks wrong (Health Canada, USU, NCHFP). Low-acid food can show no sign. Wear gloves. Bag swollen jars. Boil unsealed or leaking ones, covered by 2.5 cm (1 in) of water, for 30 minutes before binning (NCHFP).

## Storing water
- **Amount:** 2 L per person per day to drink, plus 2 L for cooking and cleaning, for at least 72 hours (Health Canada). US: 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day (Ready.gov).
- **Containers:** food-grade, washed, then sanitized with 1 tsp (5 mL) unscented bleach per quart (about 1 L). Replace home-filled water every 6 months (Ready.gov).
- **Treat:** rolling boil 1 minute, 3 minutes above 1,500 m (5,000 ft). Or 2 drops of unscented 5 to 9% bleach per litre, stirred, 30 minutes; double if cloudy. Treating does not remove fuel or chemicals (CDC).
